mission_1.route.text:
I plan to move for about 4 units to the right and also create map coverage of the opening, and see what that looks like by moving around the entrance. Then I will go inside the entrance and move around to create further map coverage by rotating around once inside the entrance.

I predict the map coverage will be weakest when the robot is in a constrained area that still has a lot of unknown map area that can only be accessible through small openings (in which case the LiDAR scan can't easily scan for).

mission_2.strategy.text: My second route will take the robot to enter through the entrance, but instead of just entering another room through the hallway, the robot will traverse the hallway back and forth. It may produce a clearer map as it will cover more overall space.

responses.final.synthesis: Based on the two maps that were generated from exploration, the robot can know about the area in the entrance, the area prior to the entrance, the area immediately after entering the entrance of the TurtleBot3 house, the hallway immediately adjacent to the area of the entrance, and generally speaking, the area that opens up from the hallway into the different rooms. It cannot know more information beyond what was mapped or what was accurately mapped in the case of strategy 2. LiDAR coverage covered quite a bit more distance in strategy 2 but was much more inaccurate in terms of mapping out actual obstacles. There was less coverage in strategy 1, but the coverage was much more accurate, and there was much more clearly free area to move in that the robot can therefore rely on. I would trust map 1 much more for the later task because it is most consistent with the actual house layout and most accurate as a result, and therefore reliable.
responses.mission_1.drift_and_revisit: When I returned to a previously scanned area, I didn't notice any change in previously mapped walls. Evidence such as periodic before-after screenshots and SLAM diagnostic data would be helpful in determining whether SLAM corrected drift.
responses.mission_1.limitations: An area that remained unknown was the area to the right side of the hallway immediately accessible through the entrance. My route was initially planned to include rotation during the time the robot was in the hallway, but the LiDAR's line of sight was only able to cover a shorter distance than I expected, so much of the area opposite the direction the robot went in remained unknown.

responses.mission_2.comparison: Route 2 gave more useful coverage for the time spent.  The prediction that the known area would increase was correct. However, the map quality decreased, which is something that's visibly seen and also seen in the quality score dropping by 2.5 points. The known area per minute increased by 0.35 m²/min, despite just an approximately 1-minute increase in elapsed time. The trade-off is that the map accuracy and quality decrease despite there being much more known area, and so the trade-off is more about usable known quantities.
responses.mission_2.map_choice:
I would trust the first strategy much more. The one limit is that, for strategy two, I did likely actually make the robot fall over, and hence some of the readings were incorrect due to this. Maybe another run would probably be much more reliable in reassessing whether strategy two was good or not.

However, I definitely would trust the first strategy much more, just because it made use of a lot more rotation to map out an area around multiple given points during the route. Additionally, the walls are clearly very aligned and follow the actual structure of the area. Despite there being some missing rooms, at least the room that is included is mapped out accurately. The limit of what these images and the numbers cannot prove is that wall positions and distances are geometrically accurate.
